record.field: Running goals with OKR: the operating rhythm
method

OKR is a rhythm, not a form. Each cycle: plan (a few objectives, each with 2–4 measurable key results, approved by the manager), run (a short check-in every week or two: current value, confidence, blockers), score (0.0–1.0 at cycle end; around 0.7 on an aspirational goal is a good outcome, committed goals are expected to land), and reset (retrospective, then roll unfinished work into the next cycle). The single most common failure is "set and forget" — goals written in January and reopened in December. The check-in cadence is what keeps this system alive.
OKR vs KPI: change the business vs run the business
method

KPIs monitor the machine: they have a normal level, a direction, and an owner, and they should stay healthy every period. OKRs change the machine: they describe the few improvements this cycle exists for. If a number must simply stay above 95%, it is a KPI. If reaching it requires new work, it belongs in an objective with key results. Keep both, and resist turning every KPI into an OKR — a scorecard full of "business as usual" drowns the few changes that matter.
The Balanced Scorecard read: four perspectives
method

Tag objectives and KPIs with a perspective — Financial, Customer, Internal Process, Learning & Growth — then group any goal list by perspective and look at the shape. A portfolio that is all Financial is borrowing against next year; nothing in Learning & Growth means the capability that produces future results is not being built. The balance check takes one minute per cycle and catches strategic blind spots early.
Key success factors: from strategy to measures
method

A key success factor is an area where things must go right for the strategy to work — "service and delivery quality", "talent retention". Keep the list short (a company has 5–8, not 30). Each objective should declare which factor it drives; each KPI should declare which factor it measures. When a factor has no measuring KPI, you are flying blind on something you called critical. When a KPI measures no factor, ask why you track it at all.
Writing key results that can be scored
measure

A key result is a number, not an activity. "Launch the new onboarding flow" is a milestone; "raise activation from 30% to 50%" is a key result. Set the baseline honestly, pick the direction (higher/lower), and choose a target where ~70% progress would still be a good quarter. Three key results per objective is usually enough; if you need six, the objective is two objectives.
Documenting a KPI so any reader trusts it
measure

Every KPI in the library carries a documentation form: business definition, calculation formula, unit, direction, aggregation (final / average / cumulative), frequency, data source, and whether it leads or lags results. Fill it once, argue about it never again. The "How to collect" guideline on each KPI tells the operator exactly which system or report the number comes from and who confirms it.
The check-in habit: value, confidence, blockers
cadence

A good check-in takes two minutes: the current value, a 1–10 confidence that the target will be reached, and the one blocker in the way. Confidence trends matter more than single values — three declining check-ins in a row is an early warning the alert engine watches for. Blockers written down become the agenda of the next review meeting automatically; blockers kept in heads become December surprises.
Collecting actuals: automatic, imported, manual
data

Numbers arrive three ways. Automatic: metric sources and the sales/project bridges pull from Odoo data on schedule. Imported: monthly CSV/Excel exports from outside systems (MES, helpdesk, analytics) land through the actuals import wizard. Manual: anything else is typed in at period close. Two rules keep the data trustworthy: manual entry always beats automation, and a period confirmed by a manager is never silently changed by any collector. Each role's collection playbook in the library says where its numbers live.
Reading pace: expected progress and run-rate
review

Halfway through the cycle, a key result at 20% is not "in progress", it is behind — the diagnosis panel compares actual progress with the share of calendar already spent and computes the run-rate now required. A required run-rate above ~1.5× the pace so far is a signal to act: remove the recorded blocker, re-scope through a target revision with manager approval, or accept the miss consciously in the review meeting. Acting in month two is cheap; discovering in month twelve is not.
Fair scoring: calibration and the anonymity rules
review

Scores are compared across teams in a calibration session before they are final; any change requires a written justification, and applied changes are frozen — for everyone. 360° feedback is aggregated only when at least the minimum number of raters have answered, and rater identities are never shown. Keep OKR scores away from bonus formulas: pay against committed KPIs, learn from aspirational OKRs — the moment a stretch goal decides a bonus, everyone stops stretching.
Building your company knowledge on top of the library
library

Start a new team or cycle from the role library: pick your industry, pick the role, apply the pack, then edit the drafts — the templates are reference points, not prescriptions. Capture what you learn back: the capture wizard turns your own proven objectives and KPIs into company templates (kept per company, never mixed into the shared built-ins), and administrators can add articles like this one for your market. Over cycles, the library becomes your organization's own management playbook.
